p01-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: random features $\mathbf{x}$, target $y$, weights $\mathbf{w}$; residual $e=y-\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{w}$.

p01-c2-t.text:
Learning goals: derive the MSE normal equation from squared error; tell features, weights and projected output apart; verify the residual is orthogonal to every usable direction
In one line: MSE finds the linear output closest to the target, with no need to get every sample right
Like moving a shadow on a screen: the best shadow is nearest the object

p02-ctx-t.name: p02-ctx-t

p02-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: $\hat y=\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{w}$; $e=y-\hat y$; binary target $y=\pm1$; finite second moments.

Learning compares continuous outputs; only at the end do we classify by sign
A correct sign with a score far from the target still has squared error

p03-title.name: p03-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-title.text: Expand the square: zero gradient is the normal equation

p03-bridge.name: p03-bridge

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-bridge.text: Last page: $J(\mathbf{w})$. This page expands it, sets the gradient to zero, and solves for the best weights.

p03-ctx-t.name: p03-ctx-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: $R_x=E[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^T]$, $\mathbf{p}=E[\mathbf{x}y]$; the solution is unique when $R_x$ is positive definite.

p03-fig-title.name: p03-fig-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-fig-title.text: Four steps: expand, differentiate, set to zero, solve

p03-c2-t.name: p03-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-c2-t.text:
Set the gradient to zero: $R_x\hat{\mathbf{w}}=\mathbf{p}$; when $R_x$ is invertible, $\hat{\mathbf{w}}=R_x^{-1}\mathbf{p}$
$R_x$ positive definite: every nonzero feature combination has positive mean square, so the solution is unique
Covariance $\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{x})=R_x-E[\mathbf{x}]E[\mathbf{x}]^T$

p03-ban-t.name: p03-ban-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-ban-t.text: Takeaway: the normal equation R w equals p is the condition for minimum MSE.

p04-bridge.name: p04-bridge

p04-ctx-t.name: p04-ctx-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: $E[x_je]=0$ (each feature); inner product $\langle u,v\rangle=E[uv]$; prediction lies in the feature span.

p04-fig-title.name: p04-fig-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-c2-t.name: p04-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-c2-t.text:
Zero gradient rewrites as $E[x_je]=0$: the best residual is orthogonal to every feature direction and every linear combination
For any other linear prediction $\tilde y$: $E[(y-\tilde y)^2]=E[(y-\hat y)^2]+E[(\hat y-\tilde y)^2]\ge E[(y-\hat y)^2]$
The cross term vanishes by orthogonality; the second term can only add error

p04-ban-t.text: Takeaway: the projection is the closest point on the plane to the target, and the residual is perpendicular to the plane.

steps.speakerNotes: Goal: change 'separate perfectly'… · 1/3 · Female: Last unit's constraints required strict separability. If two classes overlap, the perceptron may keep correcting and never stop. Think: when the data simply cannot be separated, what else can we ask for?

narration.label: s1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Last unit's constraints required strict separability. If two classes overlap, the perceptron may keep correcting and never stop. Think: when the data simply cannot be separated, what else can we ask for?

steps.label: Goal: change 'separate perfectly'… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Goal: change 'separate perfectly'… · 2/3 · Male: Ask to get as close as possible. This unit has three goals: derive the normal equation from squared error, tell features, weights and projected outputs apart, and finally verify that the residual is perpendicular to every usable direction.

narration.label: s2.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Ask to get as close as possible. This unit has three goals: derive the normal equation from squared error, tell features, weights and projected outputs apart, and finally verify that the residual is perpendicular to every usable direction.

steps.label: Goal: change 'separate perfectly'… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Goal: change 'separate perfectly'… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: residuals are allowed, yet we can still find the linear output closest to the target. Next page, we define the mean squared error.

narration.label: s3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: residuals are allowed, yet we can still find the linear output closest to the target. Next page, we define the mean squared error.

steps.label: Mean squared error: score each… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Mean squared error: score each… · 1/3 · Male: The approach is to give each sample a target, plus 1 or minus 1 for two classes. The prediction is features times weights, a continuous number, and the residual is target minus prediction, positive or negative. Think: if the sign is right but the score is far from the target, is there error?

narration.label: s4.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: The approach is to give each sample a target, plus 1 or minus 1 for two classes. The prediction is features times weights, a continuous number, and the residual is target minus prediction, positive or negative. Think: if the sign is right but the score is far from the target, is there error?

steps.label: Mean squared error: score each… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Mean squared error: score each… · 2/3 · Female: Yes. The mean squared error J is the expected squared residual. As long as the score is far from the target, the squared error is not zero, even with the right sign. Learning compares continuous outputs, and only at the end do we classify by sign.

narration.label: s5.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Yes. The mean squared error J is the expected squared residual. As long as the score is far from the target, the squared error is not zero, even with the right sign. Learning compares continuous outputs, and only at the end do we classify by sign.

steps.label: Mean squared error: score each… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Mean squared error: score each… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: MSE measures the distance between output and target, not whether the sign is right. Next page, we expand the square and find the minimum.

narration.label: s6.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Take this away: MSE measures the distance between output and target, not whether the sign is right. Next page, we expand the square and find the minimum.

steps.label: Expand the square: zero gradient… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Expand the square: zero gradient… · 1/3 · Female: Expand J: the expectation of y squared, minus 2 times w transpose p, plus w transpose R w. R is the expected outer product of the features, and p is the expected feature times target. Predict: what do we get when we differentiate with respect to w?

narration.label: s7.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Expand J: the expectation of y squared, minus 2 times w transpose p, plus w transpose R w. R is the expected outer product of the features, and p is the expected feature times target. Predict: what do we get when we differentiate with respect to w?

steps.label: Expand the square: zero gradient… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Expand the square: zero gradient… · 2/3 · Male: The gradient is minus 2p plus 2 R w, which also equals minus 2 times the expectation of x times the residual. Set it to zero and we get the normal equation R w equals p. The source wrote the gradient with a plus sign; we correct it: since the residual is target minus prediction, differentiating brings out a minus sign.

narration.label: s8.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: The gradient is minus 2p plus 2 R w, which also equals minus 2 times the expectation of x times the residual. Set it to zero and we get the normal equation R w equals p. The source wrote the gradient with a plus sign; we correct it: since the residual is target minus prediction, differentiating brings out a minus sign.

steps.label: Expand the square: zero gradient… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Expand the square: zero gradient… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: the normal equation R w equals p is the condition for minimum MSE. If R is positive definite, the solution is unique. Next page, the geometry.

narration.label: s9.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: the normal equation R w equals p is the condition for minimum MSE. If R is positive definite, the solution is unique. Next page, the geometry.

steps.label: Zero gradient: the best residual… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Zero gradient: the best residual… · 1/3 · Male: In the figure, the thick black line is the plane spanned by the features, the blue arrow is the target y, the green arrow is its projection on the plane, and the red dashed line is the residual. Think: what angle does the residual make with the plane?

narration.label: s10.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: In the figure, the thick black line is the plane spanned by the features, the blue arrow is the target y, the green arrow is its projection on the plane, and the red dashed line is the residual. Think: what angle does the residual make with the plane?

steps.label: Zero gradient: the best residual… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Zero gradient: the best residual… · 2/3 · Female: Perpendicular. Zero gradient means the expected product of the residual with each feature is zero, so it is orthogonal to any combination of them. For any other prediction, the error splits into two terms; the cross term vanishes by orthogonality, and the second term is never negative.

narration.label: s11.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Perpendicular. Zero gradient means the expected product of the residual with each feature is zero, so it is orthogonal to any combination of them. For any other prediction, the error splits into two terms; the cross term vanishes by orthogonality, and the second term is never negative.

steps.label: Zero gradient: the best residual… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Zero gradient: the best residual… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: the projection is the closest point on the plane to the target, and the residual is perpendicular to the plane. Next page, we compute with 3D numbers.

narration.label: s12.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Take this away: the projection is the closest point on the plane to the target, and the residual is perpendicular to the plane. Next page, we compute with 3D numbers.

steps.label: 3D example: two basis vectors… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: 3D example: two basis vectors… · 1/3 · Female: We use the source demo's starting values. Both basis vectors lie in the plane where z is zero, and the target is 1.35, 0.85, 1.25. Predict: when the target drops onto the plane, which direction's distance remains?

narration.label: s13.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: We use the source demo's starting values. Both basis vectors lie in the plane where z is zero, and the target is 1.35, 0.85, 1.25. Predict: when the target drops onto the plane, which direction's distance remains?

steps.label: 3D example: two basis vectors… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: 3D example: two basis vectors… · 2/3 · Male: X transpose X has determinant 0.75, and X transpose y is about 1.35 and 1.4111. The coefficients are about 0.8593 and 0.9815, the projection is 1.35, 0.85, 0, and the residual is 0, 0, 1.25.

narration.label: s14.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: X transpose X has determinant 0.75, and X transpose y is about 1.35 and 1.4111. The coefficients are about 0.8593 and 0.9815, the projection is 1.35, 0.85, 0, and the residual is 0, 0, 1.25.

steps.label: 3D example: two basis vectors… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: 3D example: two basis vectors… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: the residual is only the perpendicular 1.25, with zero inner product against both basis vectors. Note the coefficients are two-dimensional and the target and projection are three-dimensional; do not mix them up. Next page, the picture.

narration.label: s15.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: the residual is only the perpendicular 1.25, with zero inner product against both basis vectors. Note the coefficients are two-dimensional and the target and projection are three-dimensional; do not mix them up. Next page, the picture.

steps.label: Picturing the projection: the… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Picturing the projection: the… · 1/3 · Male: This is a side view. Horizontal is the plane, vertical is the z direction. The blue arrow is the target, height 1.25; the green arrow is its projection on the plane. Guess: what angle does the red dashed line make with the plane?

narration.label: s16.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: This is a side view. Horizontal is the plane, vertical is the z direction. The blue arrow is the target, height 1.25; the green arrow is its projection on the plane. Guess: what angle does the red dashed line make with the plane?

steps.label: Picturing the projection: the… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Picturing the projection: the… · 2/3 · Female: Ninety degrees. The target drops perpendicularly onto the plane, so the residual length is 1.25 and the squared residual is 1.5625, the smallest squared error among all points on the plane. The near-zero inner products from code are just floating-point scale.

narration.label: s17.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Ninety degrees. The target drops perpendicularly onto the plane, so the residual length is 1.25 and the squared residual is 1.5625, the smallest squared error among all points on the plane. The near-zero inner products from code are just floating-point scale.

steps.label: Picturing the projection: the… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Picturing the projection: the… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: the target drops perpendicularly onto the plane, and the squared residual 1.5625 is the minimum error. Next page, multiple outputs and the common myth.

narration.label: s18.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Take this away: the target drops perpendicularly onto the plane, and the squared residual 1.5625 is the minimum error. Next page, multiple outputs and the common myth.

steps.label: Myth: the best projection means… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Myth: the best projection means… · 1/3 · Female: A common myth: since it is the best projection, is the residual zero? Is the error rate the lowest? Think: was the residual zero in the example just now?

narration.label: s19.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: A common myth: since it is the best projection, is the residual zero? Is the error rate the lowest? Think: was the residual zero in the example just now?

steps.label: Myth: the best projection means… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Myth: the best projection means… · 2/3 · Male: No. The residual need not be zero, and the smallest squared error does not mean the lowest error rate. With M classes, set the target vector to 1 at the right class and 0 elsewhere; each weight column serves one class, and the squared norm splits into M scalar problems.

narration.label: s20.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: No. The residual need not be zero, and the smallest squared error does not mean the lowest error rate. With M classes, set the target vector to 1 at the right class and 0 elsewhere; each weight column serves one class, and the squared norm splits into M scalar problems.

steps.label: Myth: the best projection means… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Myth: the best projection means… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: MSE finds the output closest to the target, with no guarantee of zero residual or fewest mistakes. When feature directions repeat, R may be singular; the best prediction still exists, but the weights are not unique. Now your turn.

narration.label: s21.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: MSE finds the output closest to the target, with no guarantee of zero residual or fewest mistakes. When feature directions repeat, R may be singular; the best prediction still exists, but the weights are not unique. Now your turn.

steps.label: Practice: the basis becomes the… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Practice: the basis becomes the… · 1/3 · Male: Your turn. The basis is now the two coordinate axes, and the target is 2, minus 1, 3. Find the coefficients, projection and residual, and check the inner products. Hint: write the two columns of X first, then solve the normal equation.

narration.label: s22.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Your turn. The basis is now the two coordinate axes, and the target is 2, minus 1, 3. Find the coefficients, projection and residual, and check the inner products. Hint: write the two columns of X first, then solve the normal equation.

steps.label: Practice: the basis becomes the… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Practice: the basis becomes the… · 2/3 · Female: X transpose X is the identity, so the coefficients are X transpose y, which is 2 and minus 1. The projection is 2, minus 1, 0, the residual is 0, 0, 3, the inner products are all zero, and the squared residual is 9.

narration.label: s23.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: X transpose X is the identity, so the coefficients are X transpose y, which is 2 and minus 1. The projection is 2, minus 1, 0, the residual is 0, 0, 3, the inner products are all zero, and the squared residual is 9.

steps.label: Practice: the basis becomes the… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Practice: the basis becomes the… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: with the axis basis, the projection just drops the third coordinate. Next question: real data often have unknown expectations, so what then? The next unit replaces the expectation with single samples, the LMS algorithm.

narration.label: s24.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Take this away: with the axis basis, the projection just drops the third coordinate. Next question: real data often have unknown expectations, so what then? The next unit replaces the expectation with single samples, the LMS algorithm.
